bio.en: Nicole Forsgren is the developer productivity expert behind Accelerate and DORA metrics, helping organizations measure and improve how engineering teams deliver software.
bio.zh: 妮可·福斯格伦（Nicole Forsgren）是《Accelerate》与 DORA 指标背后的开发者生产力专家，帮助组织衡量并改进工程团队交付软件的方式。

summary.en: Nicole stresses starting with a crisp definition of the problem or goal, since ambiguity is the biggest challenge even at executive levels. She explains the DORA metrics and why measuring outcomes beats activity. The episode is a practical guide to diagnosing and improving developer experience and team performance.
summary.zh: 妮可强调，要从清晰定义"问题或目标"开始，因为模糊性即便在高管层也是最大的挑战。她解释了 DORA 指标，以及为何衡量结果优于衡量活动。本期是一份关于诊断并改进开发者体验与团队绩效的实用指南。

turns.speaker: Nicole Forsgren
turns.en: Starting with what is your problem or what is your goal? I would say this is a bigger challenge than most people recognize or realize. 80% of the folks that I work with, this is their biggest problem. Even at executive levels, teams will have gone off for several months, and they're tackling something, and they'll come back with uncertainty, and they'll say like, "Well, you told me to improve developer experience." (00:00:20): I'm like, "Okay, what do you mean by this? Are you talking about inner and outer loop? Are you talking about friction? Are you talking about culture? But if you're talking about culture, this is totally different than if you're talking about friction in toolchains. If you're on different pages, you're heading in completely different directions."
turns.zh: 从"你的问题是什么、你的目标是什么"开始。我会说这是一个比大多数人认识到或意识到的更大的挑战。我合作的人里 80% 都把这个问题当成他们最大的问题。即使在高管层面，团队也会花几个月去搞某个东西，然后带着不确定性回来，说类似"好吧，你让我去改善开发者体验。" (00:00:20)：我就说："好，你这话是什么意思？你说的是内循环还是外循环（inner and outer loop）？你说的是摩擦（friction）？你说的是文化？但如果你说的是文化，那和你说的工具链里的摩擦完全是两回事。如果你们不在同一个频道上，你们就走向完全不同的方向。"

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Welcome to Lenny's Podcast where I interview world-class product leaders and growth experts to learn from their hardware experiences, building and growing today's most successful products. Today my guest is Nicole Forsgren. This is actually my first recording back since going on pat leave for the past couple months, and what an awesome episode to get back into the swing of things. Nicole is the developer productivity expert, having written the award-winning book Accelerate, and she's been the co-author of the State of DevOps Report year after year. (00:01:06): She's currently a partner at Microsoft Research, leading developer productivity, research, and strategy, and she's helped some of the biggest companies in the world move faster, improved product quality, and transform their cultures. In our conversation, we get into the weeds of how to go about measuring and improving your engineering team's productivity and experience. We talk about the DORA framework and the SPACE framework and how to actually implement them to understand how your engineering team is doing. (00:01:32): Nicole also shares benchmarks for what elite companies are at. We talk about why moving faster turns out to be one of the best ways to improve quality and stability. Plus, pitfalls you want to avoid, and also a preview of a new book that she's working on, and so much more. Enjoy this episode with Nicole Forsgren after a short word from our sponsors. Today's entire episode is brought to you by DX, a platform for measuring and improving developer productivity. DX is designed by the researchers behind frameworks such as DORA SPACE and DevX, including Nicole Forsgren, who is my guest for this very episode. (00:02:09): If you've tried measuring developer productivity, you know that there are a lot of basic metrics out there and a lot of ways to do this wrong, and getting that full view of productivity is still really hard. DX tackles this problem by combining qualitative and quantitative insights based on the very research Nicole and her team have done, giving you full clarity into how your developers are doing. DX is used by both startups and Fortune 500 companies, including companies like Twilio, Amplitude, eBay, Brex, Toast, Pfizer, and Procter & Gamble. To learn more about DX and get a demo of their product, visit their website at getdx.com/lenny. That's getdx.com/lenny. Nicole, welcome to the podcast.
turns.zh: 欢迎来到 Lenny 的播客，在这里我采访世界级的产品负责人和增长专家，从他们打造并增长当今最成功产品的实战经验中学习。今天的嘉宾是 Nicole Forsgren。这其实是我过去几个月休陪产假（pat leave）回来后的第一场录制，而能回到节奏里、录这样一期精彩的节目真是太好了。Nicole 是开发者生产力专家，写过获奖书籍《Accelerate》，并且年复一年地担任《State of DevOps Report》（DevOps 现状报告）的合著者。 (00:01:06)：她目前是微软研究院（Microsoft Research）的合伙人，领导开发者生产力、研究与战略，并且帮助过世界上一些最大的公司更快地前进、提升产品质量、并转型他们的文化。在我们的对话中，我们深入探讨如何衡量并改善你的工程团队的生产力和体验。我们聊了 DORA 框架和 SPACE 框架，以及如何真正落地它们来理解你的工程团队做得怎么样。 (00:01:32)：Nicole 还分享了精英公司的基准数据。我们聊了为什么"更快地前进"其实是提升质量和稳定性的最好方式之一。此外还有你想避开的陷阱，以及她正在写的一本新书的前瞻，以及更多内容。在赞助商简短介绍之后，请享受这期与 Nicole Forsgren 的节目。本期整集由 DX 赞助，一个衡量并改善开发者生产力的平台。DX 由 DORA、SPACE、DevX 等框架背后的研究者设计，包括本期的嘉宾 Nicole Forsgren。 (00:02:09)：如果你试过衡量开发者生产力，你知道市面上有很多基础指标、也有很多做错的方式，而获得生产力的全貌仍然非常难。DX 通过结合定性和定量的洞察——基于 Nicole 和她团队所做的那些研究——来解决这个问题，让你完全清楚地了解你的开发者做得怎么样。DX 被创业公司和财富 500 强公司使用，包括 Twilio、Amplitude、eBay、Brex、Toast、Pfizer、Procter & Gamble 这样的公司。要了解更多关于 DX 的信息并获取产品演示，请访问他们的网站 getdx.com/lenny。就是 getdx.com/lenny。Nicole，欢迎来到播客。

turns.speaker: Nicole Forsgren
turns.en: Thank you so much. I'm excited to be here.
turns.zh: 非常感谢。我很兴奋来到这里。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: I'm excited to have you here. I actually skip this question usually with guests, but I thought it'd be actually really valuable to spend a little time on your background. You have such a unique role and unique set of experiences. Could you just talk briefly about the things you've been up to in your career, where you've worked, and then what you're up to now and what you focus on these days?
turns.zh: 我很高兴你在这里。我其实通常都会跳过这个问题，但我觉得花点时间聊你的背景其实很有价值。你有这么独特的角色和独特的经历组合。你能简要聊聊你职业生涯里做过的事、在哪些地方工作过，然后你现在在做什么、最近聚焦在什么上面吗？

turns.speaker: Nicole Forsgren
turns.en: Sure, and I appreciate the question because you're right. I sort of had this choose your own adventure background. So I started as a software engineer at IBM. I was writing software for large enterprise systems, which meant I ended up running them. So I was also a CIS admin. I was racking the stacking. I was running these really, really large labs, and then I kind of stumbled into this seven-day march for several years, and I was like, "There has to be a better way." And we're hearing rumors of it, but management was not buying in. And so I decided to win this battle with data, and I was like, "I should go do a Ph.D." (00:03:55): And so ended up kind of taking a slight pivot into Ph.D. and management information systems, which some people are less familiar with, but it's basically a cross between tech and business. And I ended up getting a fairly technical Ph.D. So I went to a school, I went to University of Arizona, which has a very, very technical degree, but I liked that it crossed with business because then I had the ability to make these strong business case statements, right. So it was like, how is or is the way that we develop and deliver software tied to outcomes at the individual level, right? (00:04:33): Can I be more productive? Can I have better work-life balance? And the team level, is the team more productive? Is the team more efficient? And the organizational level, right. This is what I was really interested in originally. Do I see better ROI? Do I see better efficiency because then I could sell it to people, right? And so that was really kind of what I originally went into. And then I was a professor for a handful of years because if you're doing research, traditionally, that's the job in academia. I also had a master's in accounting because that really helped me make that kind of financial tie and understanding financial statements. (00:05:07): And then, after a handful of years kind of walked away from tenure because academia was not convinced that DevOps was a thing, right, that DevOps wasn't real, and State of DevOps Report who I was doing with DORA, DevOps research and assessment in collaboration with Jez Humble and Gene Kim. And we started that work with Puppet. So shout out to Alanna Brown for starting that, and Nigel Kersten and the team there. We kind of pivoted away. And Chef, that little configuration management startup at the time, hired me, and they're like, "We'll give you halftime to do research and halftime to help our engineering practices improve."
turns.zh: 当然，我很感激这个问题，因为你是对的。我有点像是有一段"自选冒险"式的背景。我最初是 IBM 的软件工程师。我为大型企业系统写软件，这意味着我最后也要去运行它们。所以我也是个 CIS（计算机信息系统）管理员。我在做机架堆叠。我运行着这些非常非常大的实验室，然后我有点误打误撞地陷入了这种"七年长征"（seven-day march）好几年，我就想："肯定有更好的方式。"我们也听到过这方面的传言，但管理层不买账。所以我决定用数据来赢得这场战斗，我就想："我应该去读个博士。" (00:03:55)：所以最后有点转向了读博士，方向是管理信息系统（management information systems），有些人不太熟悉这个，但它本质上是技术和商业的交叉。我最后拿了一个相当偏技术的博士。所以我去了亚利桑那大学（University of Arizona），它有一个非常非常技术化的学位，但我喜欢它和商业交叉，因为那样我就有能力做出这些强有力的商业论证（business case），对吧。所以就像是，我们开发和交付软件的方式，是否、以及如何与个体层面的结果挂钩，对吧？ (00:04:33)：我能更有生产力吗？我能有更好的工作生活平衡吗？在团队层面，团队更有生产力吗？团队更高效吗？在组织层面，对吧。这是我最初真正感兴趣的。我能看到更好的投资回报率（ROI）吗？我能看到更好的效率，因为那样我就能把它卖给别人，对吧？所以那其实是我最初进入这个领域的初衷。然后我做了几年教授，因为如果你做研究，传统上那是学术界的职位。我还有一个会计硕士，因为那真的帮我建立了那种财务上的联系、并理解财务报表。 (00:05:07)：然后，几年后我有点放弃了终身教职（tenure），因为学术界并不相信 DevOps 是个真东西，对吧，认为 DevOps 不真实；而我当时和 DORA（DevOps 研究与评估）一起做的《State of DevOps Report》，是和 Jez Humble、Gene Kim 合作的。我们最初是在 Puppet 的时候开始的这项工作。所以要感谢 Alanna Brown 启动了它，还有 Nigel Kersten 和那边的团队。我们后来有点转向了。然后 Chef——当时那家小小的配置管理创业公司——雇了我，他们说："我们给你一半时间做研究，一半时间帮我们改善工程实践。"

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: That's cool.
turns.zh: 那很酷。

turns.speaker: Nicole Forsgren
turns.en: Yeah. I mean, they were incredible because what startup is going to be like, "Yeah, do research." So I was there for a year and a half and then left to do DORA full-time. We actually had a SaaS offering, so we continued the State of DevOps Report just under the DORA banner, and we had a SaaS offering because so many large companies were like, "I want my own customized measurement, reading, and report." And then the joke there when we met with Gartner, they were like, "Your superpower here was that you tricked people into strategy," which was not only how do I benchmark? That was kind of our top-of-the-funnel. Everyone wants to know how they compare. (00:06:22): But the important thing is what should you do next? What's the most important next step? So it's how do I measure? What do I do next? And that gave me this incredible view into advising large organizations into this transformation journey. And then, we built out this amazing partner network. We weren't actually consulting. We just had this SaaS piece, but then how do you act on it? We were then acquired by Google, so I was CEO. And so I kind of led that acquisition and then the integration and building out these teams in Google. And after that point, I joined GitHub, which is the largest developer network. (00:07:01): So I had this amazing opportunity to do more grounded and applied research again. I was VP of research and strategy and then went over to MSR, where I kind of wear a couple of hats. So right now, I have a research lab there with an incredible team. It's the developer experience lab where we do a bunch of work across productivity, community, and wellbeing. And then I also help with Microsoft's kind of cross company effort to improve their developer infrastructure. So it's sort of this round effort into how do I really remain engaged in measuring, applying, thinking about this work, both in very applied concrete pieces and incredibly forward-looking work with MSR.
turns.zh: 对。我是说，他们不可思议，因为哪家创业公司会像"对，去做研究吧"。所以我在那里待了一年半，然后离开去全职做 DORA。我们实际上有一个 SaaS 产品，所以我们继续在 DORA 的旗号下做《State of DevOps Report》，而且我们有 SaaS 产品，因为那么多大公司都说："我想要我自己定制的测量、解读和报告。"然后我们和 Gartner 开会时有个笑话，他们说："你们在这里的超能力是你们骗人们进入了战略，"也就是不只是"我怎么对标？"那有点像我们的漏斗顶端。每个人都想知道自己比得怎么样。 (00:06:22)：但重要的是下一步该做什么？最重要的一步是什么？所以是"我怎么衡量？我下一步做什么？"而这给了我一个不可思议的视角，去给大型组织做转型之旅的顾问。然后，我们建立了这个很棒的合作伙伴网络。我们其实不是在咨询。我们只有这个 SaaS 部件，但然后你该怎么行动？我们随后被 Google 收购，所以我是 CEO。所以我有点领导了那次收购，然后是整合、在 Google 里组建这些团队。在那之后，我加入了 GitHub，那是最大的开发者网络。 (00:07:01)：所以我有了这个不可思议的机会，再次做更接地气、更应用的研究。我是研究与战略副总裁，然后去了 MSR（微软研究院），在那里我戴了好几顶帽子。所以现在，我有一个在那里的研究实验室，有一个很棒的团队。那是开发者体验实验室（developer experience lab），我们在生产力、社区和幸福感（wellbeing）方面做一堆工作。然后我也帮忙微软那种跨公司的、改善他们开发者基础设施的努力。所以这是一种全面的努力，让我如何在非常应用、具体的部分，以及和 MSR 一起极具前瞻性的工作上，都真正保持参与、衡量、应用、思考这项工作。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Amazing. And just to clarify, MSR, is that Microsoft? That's a division-
turns.zh: 太棒了。只是澄清一下，MSR，是微软吗？那是微软的一个部门——

turns.speaker: Nicole Forsgren
turns.en: Ah.
turns.zh: 啊。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: ... of Microsoft.
turns.zh: ……微软的。

turns.speaker: Nicole Forsgren
turns.en: Yeah. Thank you. Yeah, MSR is Microsoft Research.
turns.zh: 对。谢谢。对，MSR 是 Microsoft Research（微软研究院）。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Okay, cool. So you've shared a couple of these terms, DevOps, developer productivity. I'm curious what the term you like to use for this area you focus on. Developer productivity, developer experience, DevOps, what's kind of the way the best way to think about this?
turns.zh: 好，酷。所以你分享过几个术语，DevOps、开发者生产力。我好奇你喜欢用哪个词来指代你聚焦的这个领域。开发者生产力、开发者体验、DevOps，最好的思考方式是什么？

turns.speaker: Nicole Forsgren
turns.en: I really love that you asked this question because I think they're very related concepts that people sometimes conflate, but I see them as being different. So related, but different. So productivity, I think, is basically how much we can get done and how much we can do over time. And I think that's why it's so important to have this holistic measure because we can't just brute force it, right. And so that's why when my team and a bunch of my peers study productivity, we include this community effect because software is a team sport. We joke, right. (00:08:40): And also why wellbeing is so important, right. Because we see that when you do productivity the right way, we see sustainability, we see wellbeing, we see reductions in burnout. Now, developer experience is very related and very tied to this, and it contributes to productivity. But developer experiences, if you think about who your users are, developers really are you your users in this software engineering, in the software development piece. And so developer experience is sort of like what is it like to write software? Is this a friction-free process? Is this a very predictable and certain experience? Can we reduce this uncertainty and increase the predictability here to contribute to productivity?
turns.zh: 我真的很喜欢你问这个问题，因为我觉得它们是人们有时会混淆的、非常相关的概念，但我认为它们是不同的。所以相关，但不同。生产力（productivity），我觉得，基本上就是我们能干多少、随着时间能完成多少。而我觉得这就是为什么有一个整体的衡量这么重要，因为我们不能只是 brute force（硬来），对吧。所以这就是为什么当我的团队和我的一批同行研究生产力时，我们把这种社区效应（community effect）包含进来，因为软件是一项团队运动。我们开玩笑说，对吧。 (00:08:40)：也是为什么幸福感（wellbeing）这么重要，对吧。因为我们看到，当你以正确的方式做生产力时，我们看到可持续性、看到幸福感、看到职业倦怠（burnout）的减少。现在，开发者体验（developer experience）和这个非常相关、非常绑定，并且它贡献于生产力。但开发者体验，如果你想想你的用户是谁，开发者在软件工程、在软件开发这个环节里，真的就是你的用户。所以开发者体验有点像：写软件是什么感觉？这是一个无摩擦的过程吗？这是一个非常可预测、确定的体验吗？我们能否减少这种不确定性、增加这里的可预测性，从而贡献于生产力？

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: And then how does DevOps fit into that just so that we kind of have the mental model of these terms?
turns.zh: 然后 DevOps 是怎么融入其中的，好让我们在脑海里对这些术语有个心智模型？

turns.speaker: Nicole Forsgren
turns.en: People have sort of co-opted the term. So some people name their tools DevOps. I'm maybe a little more old school. So when I was doing a bunch of my DevOps research, it was the capabilities and tools and processes that we can use to improve our software development and delivery end to end so that it's faster and it is more reliable. So DevOps was kind of this technical, architectural, cultural practices that enable us to do this work better so that it is, yes, more productive, we have a better developer experience. It was kind of, again, this very holistic picture.
turns.zh: 人们有点把这个词给占用了（co-opted）。所以有些人把他们的工具命名为 DevOps。我可能更老派一点。所以当我做我那一批 DevOps 研究时，它指的是我们可以用来端到端改善软件开发和交付的能力、工具和流程，让它更快、更可靠。所以 DevOps 有点像是这种技术的、架构的、文化的实践，让我们能把这项工作做得更好，从而是的，更有生产力、有更好的开发者体验。它再次，是这种非常整体的图景。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: So what I love about this topic is that I've never met a founder or a leader who is not thinking, "We need to move faster. We need our engineers to be more productive. We need to get things out the door quicker. We want engineers to be happier." Nobody doesn't want that. And so that's why I'm excited to dig into a lot of these things. Is that roughly what you find as well, that nobody's ever like, "We're good. We don't need any of this. We don't need to focus on this area?"
turns.zh: 所以我喜欢这个话题的一点是，我从未遇到过一个创始人或领导者不在想："我们需要更快。我们需要工程师更有生产力。我们需要更快地推出东西。我们希望工程师更开心。"没有人不想这样。所以这就是我为什么兴奋地想深入聊很多这些东西。你大概也发现是这样吧——没有人会说"我们挺好的。我们不需要任何这些。我们不需要聚焦在这个领域"？

turns.speaker: Nicole Forsgren
turns.en: You know what, I'll say yes and, right. So and it kind of goes back to why I got into this because, on the one hand, you won't say anyone who's saying, "Uh, we don't really need to go faster. Everything's fine." But at the same time, very often, I will come into scenarios where I'll find myself in scenarios where people are like, "I mean, it would be nice if we were going faster, but do we really need to. Show me the business case. What's the ROI?" Or if we go too fast, we'll have an instability, right. What are our safety measures? Are we going to lose reliability? What is happening? (00:11:13): And when I first started ITIL and ITSM, right, the old school kind of change management processes, the common knowledge was that you had to have at least a two-week wait for change approvals in order to get that stability. Turns out that's not right. It was just kind of an old wives' tale, right. And so we kind of have this weird balance of I want to move faster, but is it worth the investment? What am I going to get for it? Are you sure this is the priority? Or I've been in meetings where it's like, "Oh yes, absolutely, right. This is a priority, but it's the lowest priority." (00:12:00): And I'm like... Right. So then what we want to do is we want to have these kind of pointed conversations or these kind of Socratic type questions and conversations where it's like, "Help me understand more what your concerns are. Are your concerns around reliability when you move faster?" We're not just trying to all the guardrails down and sprint for no purpose of sprinting. And this is where kind of the DORA and DevOps research program comes into play where it's we don't just want to move fast and take all guardrails down. (00:12:33): We want to implement good technical practices like automated testing, good architectural practices so that when you move fast, you are also more stable, right. We want to be thinking about improving the developer experience so that when we are faster, we are also saving time. And then, we can highlight a handful of statistics. Like, what is your typical time for feature delivery? What is your typical time to first PR? What is your typical time to steady state productivity? (00:13:04): What is your typical time for code review and PR process? And if we are to do back-of-the-napkin math, what sorts of time are you spending here? (00:14:40): And then the stability metrics are MTTR, mean time to restore. So if something happens, how long does it take you to come back? And then change fail rate. (00:16:36): And sometimes people were waiting, "If two weeks is good, a month must be better, or three months must be better, or six months must be better." turns.zh: 所以无论哪种说法都成立。在我感觉特别刻薄（snarky）的日子里，我会说"挑你的借口吧。你有个下拉菜单。"现在我说"零售业有点像个离群值"，他们有统计显著性的差异。他们的差异是，他们实际上更好。为什么？现在，我没法告诉你为什么。我可以……在一篇研究论文里，我们会有一个讨论部分，而那正是你可以猜的地方。我会推测——我们在报告里也这么做——那大概是因为零售业经历了"零售末日"（retail apocalypse），对吧。 (00:24:09)：如果你没活下来，如果你不是真的表现极佳，你就没活下来。那么多零售公司就是没熬过去。你必须在你的领域处于顶尖。没有那种……黑色星期五，没有"系统表现不极佳"这回事。没有"不在云上"这回事，因为如果你无法按需爆发（bursting）、像魔法一样爆发——有时我开玩笑说，对吧——你就活不下来。所以我怀疑，如果让我猜，如果你在零售业里还不是高表现者，自然选择已经把你淘汰了。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: That is really interesting. That makes a lot of sense. So I'm looking at these thresholds again, and I'm thinking from the perspective of a founder who's just like, "I wish my engineering team would faster." Essentially you're saying if deploy times... if they deploy more than once a day if their deploy frequencies on demand or I think it was hourly was kind of the other bucket, was that part of it?
turns.zh: 那真的很有意思。那很有道理。所以我再看这些阈值，并且从一个就想着"我希望我的工程团队更快"的创始人的视角想。本质上你说的是，如果部署时间……如果他们每天部署超过一次，如果他们的部署频率是按需——或者我想"每小时"是另一个桶，那是其中一部分吗？

turns.speaker: Nicole Forsgren
turns.en: Mm-hmm.
turns.zh: 嗯。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Yeah. And then, their mean time to their fail rate is less than 10%, and their mean time to recovery is less than an hour. Basically you're doing great. That's kind of the message of this framework, at least.
turns.zh: 对。然后，他们的平均失败率是低于 10%，他们的平均恢复时间（mean time to recovery）是低于一小时。基本上你做得很好。那大概就是这个框架的信息，至少。

turns.speaker: Nicole Forsgren
turns.en: And if you're not doing it through brute force and killing yourself. Now can I jump in here, please? Because then people are like, "But how do I do this?" So let's say that you're not in that category, and you're like because this is the next... this is the piece of criticism I'll get about DORA, right. People are like, "Well, all you've done is make me feel bad. You gave me these metrics. You've judged me. Now I feel bad." And then I'm like, "So there's DORA there." I wrote a book called Accelerate, which is the first four years of the research compiled and put together and expanded in a few things. (00:26:06): And I'll joke, "There's a whole rest of the book, right." DORA is best known for the four metrics, but there's an entire research program supporting it. So it's not just these four metrics. What we find is that if you improve a set of capabilities... I loved your question around what is DevOps? DevOps is not a toolchain you buy. Marketing teams labeled toolchains DevOps because they wanted your money. DevOps is a set of capabilities. They're technical capabilities. They're architectural capabilities. (00:26:34): They're cultural capabilities. They are lean management practices that predict speed and stability. And then speed and stability gives you money, right, because it's your ability to create these features that give you money. So when you work backwards, if you want money, you get the features fast. If you want the features fast and stable, you do the things. And the things are technical capabilities like automated testing, CI/CD.
turns.zh: 而且如果你不是通过 brute force、把自己累死来做到的话。现在我能不能插一句，拜托？因为然后人们会说"但我怎么做到这个？"所以假设你不在那个类别里，而你说——因为这是下一个……这是我会收到的关于 DORA 的批评的一部分，对吧。人们说"好吧，你所做的只是让我感觉糟糕。你给了我这些指标。你评判了我。现在我感觉糟糕。"然后我就说"所以 DORA 在那儿。"我写了一本书叫《Accelerate》，是前四年研究的汇编、整合、以及几处扩展。 (00:26:06)：我会开玩笑说"书还有一整本剩下的，对吧。"DORA 最出名的是四个指标，但支撑它的是一个完整的研究项目。所以它不只是这四个指标。我们发现的是，如果你改善一组能力……我喜欢你那个关于"DevOps 是什么"的问题。DevOps 不是你买的工具链。营销团队把工具链贴上 DevOps 的标签，因为他们想要你的钱。DevOps 是一组能力。它们是技术能力。它们是架构能力。 (00:26:34)：它们是文化能力。它们是预测速度和稳定性的精益管理实践（lean management practices）。然后速度和稳定性给你钱，对吧，因为它就是你去创造那些给你带来钱的功能的能力。所以当你倒推时，如果你想要钱，你就快速拿到功能。如果你想要快速且稳定的功能，你就去做那些事。而那些事就是技术能力，比如自动化测试、CI/CD。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: And CI/CD is continuous integration/continuous deployment, is that right?
turns.zh: 而 CI/CD 是持续集成/持续部署（continuous integration/continuous deployment），对吧？

turns.speaker: Nicole Forsgren
turns.en: Yes. Mm-hmm. Trunk based development using a version control system, right. So do you have good technical practices? Do you have good architectural practices? Do you have a loosely coupled system? Are you using the cloud? Or if you're not in the cloud for whatever reason, are you using the underlying architectural pieces that enable good cloud to do the cloud, right? Or if you're in the cloud and you're not realizing benefits, is it because doing the cloud wrong, right? Do you have a good culture? (00:27:48): So you don't just magically go fast and have stability. So working backwards, which pieces are you struggling on? Now you kind of noted down the benchmarks. If you go to dora.dev, the team at Google was lovely. We worked really closely with the team, and they're keeping this updated. You can take a quick check. There's a button there that says, "Quick check." And you can plug in where you kind of think you are. (00:28:13): Like I said, you can hunch it, and it'll tell you where you are in the benchmarks today and what industry you're in. And then the cool part is it'll say... Now you'll want to ask yourself, "Where am I struggling?" But it'll say, "For your performance profile and for the industry that you're in, statistically over the last several years, these are probably your constraints, AKA, these are probably the things that you're struggling in right now." For people in finance who are high performers, they tend to struggle with these four things, whether it's like culture or continuous integration or whatever.
turns.zh: 对。嗯。使用版本控制系统的主干开发（trunk based development），对吧。所以你有好的技术实践吗？你有好的架构实践吗？你有一个松耦合（loosely coupled）的系统吗？你在使用云吗？或者如果你因为某种原因不在云上，你在使用那些能让好的云去做云的下层架构部件吗，对吧？或者如果你在云上却没实现收益，是因为云用错了，对吧？你有好的文化吗？ (00:27:48)：所以你不是神奇地就变快、拥有了稳定性。所以倒推，你挣扎在哪些部分？现在你大概记下了基准。如果你去 dora.dev，Google 的团队很棒。我们和团队紧密合作，他们在持续更新。你可以做个快速检查。那有个按钮写着"Quick check（快速检查）"。你可以填进去你认为自己大概在哪里。 (00:28:13)：就像我说的，你可以估一下，它会告诉你今天你在基准里的哪个位置、以及你在哪个行业。然后酷的部分是它会说……现在你会想问自己"我在哪里挣扎？"但它会说"对于你的表现画像和你所在的行业，根据过去几年的统计数据，这些大概就是你的约束，也就是这些大概就是你此刻正在挣扎的事。"对于金融领域的高表现者，他们往往挣扎在这四件事上，无论是像文化还是持续集成，还是别的什么。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: I love that you're getting tactical with how to actually improve these already, which is the bread and butter of this podcast.
turns.zh: 我喜欢你已经在实际地变得战术化、讲怎么真正改善这些，这正是这档播客的看家本领。

turns.speaker: Nicole Forsgren
turns.en: Mm-hmm.
turns.zh: 嗯。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: And so we'll link to this quick check. [inaudible 00:29:02] dora.dev/quickcheck.
turns.zh: 所以我们会链接到这个快速检查。 [inaudible 00:29:02] dora.dev/quickcheck。

turns.speaker: Nicole Forsgren
turns.en: And by the way, they do not collect your name. They do not collect your info. There's no lead, lead gen, anything. Everything's just there. And then, there's deep dives into every single one of the capabilities.
turns.zh: 而且顺便说，他们不收集你的名字。他们不收集你的信息。没有线索、没有 lead gen、什么都没有。一切都就在那里。然后，还有对每个能力的深度剖析。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Amazing. And also your book talks about all these things. So people should go check out the book. Obviously it's on Amazon. Search Accelerate. Is that right?
turns.zh: 太棒了。而且你的书也讲了所有这些东西。所以人们应该去查那本书。显然它在 Amazon 上。搜 Accelerate。对吧？

turns.speaker: Nicole Forsgren
turns.en: Yep.
turns.zh: 对。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Okay. So we were talking about DORA. This may be a good time to talk about SPACE, which I think is a different framework you recommend. What is that all about?
turns.zh: 好。所以我们刚才在聊 DORA。这也许是个聊 SPACE 的好时机，我认为那是你推荐的另一个不同的框架。那是关于什么的？

turns.speaker: Nicole Forsgren
turns.en: Okay, so SPACE is a way to measure, we say productivity, developer productivity, but it's a little bit more than that. SPACE is a good way to measure any type of complex creative work. Now, how do they relate? Let's say you go through the quick check. It points out four things, and you decide you want to improve continuous integration and culture, right. Well, now you're like, "Cool, but how am I going to actually measure them?" This is where SPACE comes in because SPACE helps you figure out SPACE gives you a framework to pick the right metrics. (00:30:12): Now some people are like, "Well, SPACE you didn't give me the exact metrics." People love DORA because it's like, "Here's the exact four you need." Well, SPACE is like when you want to measure something that's complex, creative work, maybe like developer productivity. There's also an example at the bottom for incident management. When you have something you want to measure, it says, "Within your context, within the metrics you have available to you, here's how to pick." (00:30:40): That's what SPACE is good for. Now we called it SPACE because it stands for the five dimensions that you want to measure. So S is satisfaction and wellbeing. So satisfaction wellbeing is kind of self-explanatory. Now, some people might jump in here and say, "Oh, well, you're just touchy-feely." This actually matters because we find that satisfaction wellbeing ends up being incredibly highly correlated with all of the other dimensions of productivity and doing things well. (00:31:09): And as soon as satisfaction and wellbeing, things like sustainability, if you're satisfied, as soon as that starts falling off, other things start to break. So this can be an incredibly strong and important signal. P is performance. This is going to be the outcome of a process. So reliability within DORA, the MTTM or change fail rate. Those are both performance metrics.
turns.zh: 好，所以 SPACE 是一种衡量方式，我们说生产力、开发者生产力，但它比那多一点。SPACE 是衡量任何类型复杂创造性工作的好方式。那么它们怎么关联？假设你做了快速检查。它指出了四件事，而你决定想改善持续集成和文化，对吧。好，现在你会说"酷，但我到底要怎么衡量它们？"这就是 SPACE 进来的地方，因为 SPACE 帮你搞清楚——SPACE 给你一个框架来挑选正确的指标。 (00:30:12)：现在有些人会说"好吧，SPACE 你没给我确切的指标。"人们爱 DORA，因为那像是"这是你需要的确切四个。"而 SPACE 像是当你想衡量某种复杂的、创造性的工作，也许像开发者生产力。底部还有一个事件管理（incident management）的例子。当你有想衡量的东西，它说"在你的情境里、在你可用的指标里，这里是挑选的方式。" (00:30:40)：那就是 SPACE 擅长的。我们叫它 SPACE，因为它代表你想要衡量的五个维度。S 是满意度和幸福感（satisfaction and wellbeing）。所以满意度和幸福感有点不言自明。现在，有些人可能会插嘴说"哦，好吧，你就是太感情用事了。"这其实很重要，因为我们发现满意度和幸福感最终和其他所有维度都高度相关——生产力和把事情做好。 (00:31:09)：而一旦满意度和幸福感——像可持续性（sustainability）这种——如果你满意，一旦它开始下滑，其他东西就开始崩。所以这可以是一个极其强烈且重要的信号。P 是绩效（performance）。这会是某个流程的结果。所以 DORA 里的可靠性、MTTR 或变更失败率。那些都是绩效指标。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: And so you pick one to kind of measure as performance.
turns.zh: 所以你挑一个作为绩效来衡量。

turns.speaker: Nicole Forsgren
turns.en: Yep. A is activity. Anytime you have a count or a number of something. And these we see all the time because they're super easy to instrument and automate, right. Number of pull requests, number of check-ins, number of something, that's A. C is communication and collaboration. This can be how people work and talk together. It can be meetings. It can be collaboration. It can also be how our systems communicate together. It can be the searchability of a code base. And then ease efficiency and flow. So this is going to be the flow through the system. (00:32:11): It can be the time through the system. If we think about SRE or incident management, it can be the number of hops a ticket takes until it reaches the right person. Now, to use SPACE correctly, we want to use at least three dimensions at a time because that helps us balance. Turns out DORA is actually implementation of SPACE. So DORA would be SPACE for mostly that outer loop. So again, once you've found something that you want to improve, find the metrics that make sense to you, try to have them be in balance or intention so you don't throw something out of whack, but pick three.
turns.zh: 对。A 是活动（activity）。任何你有一个计数或数量的时候。这些我们一直见到，因为它们超级容易埋点和自动化，对吧。PR 的数量、签入（check-ins）的数量、某种东西的数量，那就是 A。C 是沟通与协作（communication and collaboration）。这可以是人们怎么一起工作和交谈。可以是会议。可以是协作。也可以是我们的系统怎么彼此沟通。可以是一个代码库的可搜索性。然后是 E，效率与流畅度（ease efficiency and flow）。所以这会是通过系统的流畅度。 (00:32:11)：它可以是穿过系统的时间。如果我们想 SRE 或事件管理，它可以是工单（ticket）到达正确的人之前经过的跳数（hops）。现在，要正确地使用 SPACE，我们想一次至少用三个维度，因为那帮我们平衡。结果发现 DORA 其实是 SPACE 的一种实现。所以 DORA 会是主要面向那个外循环（outer loop）的 SPACE。所以再次，一旦你找到了想改善的东西，找到对你有意义的指标，试着让它们保持平衡或有意为之，这样你不会把什么搞乱，但挑三个。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: So when you say DORA is an implementation of SPACE, one has five buckets, one has four. How do you actually think about that?
turns.zh: 所以当你说 DORA 是 SPACE 的一种实现，一个有五个桶，一个有四个。你实际上怎么思考这个？

turns.speaker: Nicole Forsgren
turns.en: So SPACE is there to help you think about how you want to pick metrics, right. So a lot of time I see people... So [inaudible 00:33:06] half step back. I used to advise people on how to pick metrics. For years people would pull me in to advise on DORA or Accelerate. They would ask me questions, but it ended up being metrics questions a lot. "How do I pick the right metrics to improve what I'm doing?" Like I said, they had the DORA numbers. They would pick their constraints, and they wanted to improve. (00:33:29): "But how do I improve? How do I measure this? How do I show improvement?" And so we would start thinking really critically about which metrics were the right metrics to pick. And I would always say make sure you pick balanced metrics. Make sure you pick metrics that are intention. And I could say it, but people have a hard time wrapping that around their heads because they kept picking things like number of lines of code, never picked number of lines of code.
turns.zh: 所以 SPACE 的存在是帮你思考你想怎么挑选指标，对吧。所以我很多时候看到人们……所以 [inaudible 00:33:06] 退半步。我以前会给人建议怎么挑指标。多年来人们会拉我进去，就 DORA 或 Accelerate 给建议。他们会问我问题，但最终很多是指标问题。"我怎么挑选正确的指标来改善我在做的事？"就像我说的，他们有 DORA 的数字。他们会挑出自己的约束，然后想改善。 (00:33:29)："但我怎么改善？我怎么衡量这个？我怎么展示改善？"所以我们会开始非常批判性地思考哪些指标是正确该挑的。而我总是说，确保你挑平衡的指标。确保你挑有意为之的指标。我能这么说，但人们很难把那个绕到脑子里，因为他们一直挑像代码行数这种东西——从来不要挑代码行数。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Oh, wow.
turns.zh: 哦，哇。

turns.speaker: Nicole Forsgren
turns.en: Number of... Still every month I get email about this.
turns.zh: 代码行数……到现在每个月我还收到关于这个的邮件。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Wow, [inaudible 00:34:00].
turns.zh: 哇，[inaudible 00:34:00]。

turns.speaker: Nicole Forsgren
turns.en: Number of pull requests, number of commits. And I was like, "These are all activity metrics." And so finally I pulled a few of my friends together and I was like, "Let's come up with a framework to help people think about it." And so there are five broad categories, pick three because that will help force you through the mental exercise of, "What could I possibly pick?" You don't need all five, right. This isn't... We're not playing-
turns.zh: PR 的数量、提交（commits）的数量。然后我就想"这些都是活动指标。"所以最后我把几个朋友拉到一起，我说"咱们想出一个框架来帮人们思考这个。"所以有五大类，挑三个，因为那会帮你被迫去做那个心理练习——"我到底可能挑什么？"你不需要全部五个，对吧。这不是……我们不是玩——

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: I see.
turns.zh: 我明白了。

turns.speaker: Nicole Forsgren
turns.en: ... bingo. We're not playing blackout bingo. You don't need all of them but try to have at least three across different dimensions. Now one example here. I was working with a group that wanted to improve their pull requests very generally. They just said improve pull requests. So they were thinking about pinging someone every 15 minutes, and I was like, "Oh, this is going to be bad." (00:34:48): Because we know from other literature and research like nursing, you'll get alert fatigue, where people will just start tuning out alerts. Either they'll turn them off, or they will just stop hearing them. So number of alerts, right. They're like, "Let's just think about number of alerts." And I said, "Well, but if we think about efficiency and flow, how much time do you have to work on your coding?" So those two are balanced. So we need to protect time to work as well as code review time.
turns.zh: ……宾果（bingo）。我们不是玩"blackout bingo（全黑宾果）"。你不需要全部，但试着至少跨不同维度有三个。现在这里有一个例子。我当时和一个小组合作，他们想很笼统地改善他们的 PR。他们只说改善 PR。所以他们考虑每 15 分钟 ping 某人一次，我就说"哦，这会很糟。" (00:34:48)：因为我们从其他文献和研究（比如护理）知道，你会有警报疲劳（alert fatigue），人们会开始无视警报。要么他们会关掉它们，要么他们就干脆不再听到它们。所以警报的数量，对吧。他们就说"咱们就想着警报数量。"我说"好吧，但如果我们想效率和流畅度，你有多少时间来做你的编码工作？"所以那两个是平衡的。所以我们需要保护工作时间以及代码审查时间。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Mm-hmm.
turns.zh: 嗯。

turns.speaker: Nicole Forsgren
turns.en: Like pull request time. And so, sometimes we can think about those, and then I think we added a satisfaction metric. Are you satisfied with the pull request process and the selection of the reviewer?
turns.zh: 像 PR 时间。所以，有时候我们可以想那些，然后我想我们加了一个满意度指标。你对 PR 流程和审查者（reviewer）的选择满意吗？

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: How do you go about actually capturing and measuring the say satisfaction?
turns.zh: 你实际上怎么去获取和衡量比如说满意度？

turns.speaker: Nicole Forsgren
turns.en: So for satisfaction, I would generally ask, right. Go ahead and ask now the ones that you instrument, you can instrument and pull out of systems all the time, right. Go ahead and grab that string. For satisfaction metric, I would only pull that periodically once every few months.
turns.zh: 所以对于满意度，我一般会去问，对吧。那些你能埋点、能一直从系统里拉出来的——就直接去抓那个数据串。对于满意度指标，我只会每隔几个月定期拉一次。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Like a survey to your engineering team.
turns.zh: 像是给你的工程团队做调查。

turns.speaker: Nicole Forsgren
turns.en: Like a survey. Yep, absolutely.
turns.zh: 像是调查。对，绝对。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Awesome.
turns.zh: 太棒了。

turns.speaker: Nicole Forsgren
turns.en: And don't discount what people say, right. Sometimes I hear... Actually not sometimes. A lot of times, I hear people say, "Oh, but people lie." First of all, what is their incentive to lie? Why would they lie about having a bad system? Because it's bad, and they want it fixed, right. If it's absolutely a hostile work environment, they might lie and then tell you it's good. Then you have bigger problems, right. Also, do we ever see bad data from our systems or incomplete data from our systems? That's a lie, but we find ways to deal with it. We see it. We acknowledge it. We look for holes in our system data. (00:36:46): We try to deal with it, right. That's also a lie. So I think there are better ways to think about and deal with that and then try to work with it because and I wrote a paper with Mik Kersten on this several years ago on how data from people and data from systems are really important compliments because we can get certain insights from people that we'll never get from systems. Let's look at lead time from changes, for example, from commit to deploy. The speed might be fine, but people might tell you it's taking absolute heroics. It's some ridiculous Rube Goldberg machine.
turns.zh: 而且不要低估人们说的话，对吧。有时我听到……其实不是有时。很多时候，我听到人们说"哦，但人们会说谎。"首先，他们说谎的动机是什么？他们为什么要对有一个糟糕的系统说谎？因为它糟糕，而他们想让它被修好，对吧。如果那绝对是个敌意的工作环境，他们可能会说谎然后告诉你它很好。那你有更大的问题了，对吧。还有，我们有没有从系统看到过坏数据、或不完整的系统数据？那也是个谎言，但我们有办法处理它。我们看到它。我们承认它。我们找系统数据里的洞。 (00:36:46)：我们试着处理它，对吧。那也是谎言。所以我觉得有更好的方式去思考和处理那个，然后试着和它一起工作，因为——几年前我和 Mik Kersten 写了一篇关于这个的论文，讲的是来自人的数据和来自系统的数据真的是重要的互补，因为我们可以从人那里得到某些我们永远无法从系统得到的洞察。比如，看看变更的交付周期，从提交到部署。速度可能没问题，但人们可能会告诉你那需要绝对的英雄之举（heroics）。那是某种荒谬的 Rube Goldberg 机器（过度复杂的装置）。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Mm-hmm.
turns.zh: 嗯。

turns.speaker: Nicole Forsgren
turns.en: The system will never tell you that. Or you could get data on your version control system. I worked with a company several years ago, and we found out that there was a significant portion of code that was just not going into any version control system. You're never going to find that out from your systems because it's not in the systems, and it was mission-critical.
turns.zh: 系统永远不可能告诉你那个。或者你可以从你的版本控制系统得到数据。几年前我和一家公司合作，我们发现有很大一部分代码根本没有进入任何版本控制系统。你永远不可能从你的系统发现那个，因为它不在系统里，而它是关键任务（mission-critical）的。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: I can see why people come to you asking for advice on metrics because you have this framework of, "Here's the type of metrics you want." And then I think, and especially from an engineering team, there's going to be this like, "How do I optimize and make sure I'm doing the right thing and measuring the right things." For someone that wants to do this, and an hour long podcast isn't going to give them all the answers, what do you recommend they go read or go do or look at to help them figure that out?
turns.zh: 我能理解为什么人们来找你问关于指标的建议，因为你有一个这样的框架——"这是你想要的那类指标。"然后我想，尤其从一个工程团队的角度，会有这种"我怎么优化、确保我做对了事、衡量对了东西。"对于一个想做这个的人，而一小时的播客没法给他们所有答案，你推荐他们去读、去做、或去看什么来帮他们搞清楚？

turns.speaker: Nicole Forsgren
turns.en: One, I hate to be this person, but I'll point to a few of my papers. It's an ACM, and I think the year we published, it was the most read paper at ACMQueue. Yeah. So we tried to make it as readable as possible. So the SPACE paper is nice because it outlines this framework and it gives examples of metrics in every single category. And so hopefully people can look at this and they can [inaudible 00:38:54], "Okay, here's an example to use here, right. Here are some of the things that I could possibly use." (00:39:00): And we're seeing that SPACE is being used lots and lots of different places. Another good one could be the paper that I mentioned with Mik Kersten, and it was about... we talked about using data from people and data from systems. We wrote it up in the DevOps context. I want to say this was written in 2016 or 2017 or something. But it helps you think through what types of data are good in which situations because you will never find yourself in a situation when you don't want both types of data. Even teams that I've worked with that are the most advanced. They have absolute instrumentation in every possible scenario. (00:39:46): In the most detailed way, they will still survey their developers at least once a year because you can get new insights, right. One book that I love. It's a little dense, but it's really interesting that I love is How to Measure Anything. And it's by Hubbard, and there are parts of it that are real stats heavy, but he has this portion in the front that's in covering intangibles. So it's like, what happens when you don't have data? You have no data. You're starting from nothing. What are good ways to hunch data? And I really love that because he covers some really good ground there.
turns.zh: 第一，我讨厌做这种人，但我会指向我的几篇论文。我会说我把东西写下来，是因为我被问得太频繁了，而我想确保它是广泛适用或广泛可得的，我想。这篇 SPACE 论文，绝对。它是 ACM 的，而且我想我们发表那年，它是 ACM Queue 上阅读量最高的论文。是的。所以我们尽量让它尽可能易读。所以 SPACE 论文很好，因为它勾勒了这个框架，并给出了每一类里的指标例子。所以希望人们能看这个，他们能 [inaudible 00:38:54] "好，这是这里可以用的一个例子，对吧。这是一些我可能能用的东西。" (00:39:00)：而且我们看到 SPACE 正在很多很多不同的地方被使用。另一篇好的是我提到的和 Mik Kersten 合写的论文，它是关于……我们聊了使用来自人的数据和来自系统的数据。我们在 DevOps 的语境下把它写下来。我想说这是 2016 或 2017 年左右写的。但它帮你想清楚在什么情况下哪种数据好，因为你永远不会遇到一种你不想同时拥有两类数据的情况。即使是我合作过的最先进的团队。他们在每种可能的场景里都有绝对的埋点。 (00:39:46)：以最详细的方式，他们仍然至少每年调查他们的开发者一次，因为你能得到新的洞察，对吧。我很喜欢的一本书。它有点晦涩（dense），但我很喜欢、真的很有意思的是《How to Measure Anything》（如何衡量任何事）。它是 Hubbard 写的，其中有部分真的统计很重，但他前面有一块是讲无形资产的。所以就像是，当你没有数据时会发生什么？你没数据。你从零开始。有哪些好的方式去大致估计数据？我真的很爱那个，因为他在那里覆盖了一些真的很好的领域。

turns.zh: 本期整集由 DX 赞助，一个衡量并改善开发者生产力的平台。DX 由 DORA、SPACE、DevX 等框架背后的研究者设计，包括本期的嘉宾 Nicole Forsgren。如果你试过衡量开发者生产力，你知道市面上有很多基础指标、也有很多做错的方式，而获得生产力的全貌仍然非常难。 (00:40:59)：DX 通过结合定性和定量的洞察——基于 Nicole 和她团队所做的那些研究——来解决这个问题，让你完全清楚地了解你的开发者做得怎么样。DX 被创业公司和财富 500 强公司使用，包括 Twilio、Amplitude、eBay、Brex、Toast、Pfizer、Procter & Gamble 这样的公司。要了解更多关于 DX 的信息并获取产品演示，请访问他们的网站 getdx.com/lenny。就是 getdx.com/lenny。你之前离线时也提到，你也许在写一本能回答很多这些问题的书。那是你愿意聊的吗？

turns.speaker: Nicole Forsgren
turns.en: Yeah, absolutely. So as I mentioned, I tend to write things down when I get asked questions on it a lot. And so this is one in particular. So we'll be covering... I'm starting to go through, and I'm covering some of these, and I think some of the important topics in particular are starting with what is your problem or what is your goal and being super, super crisp on it, right. What is it that we're trying to answer? And I would say this is a bigger challenge than most people recognize or realize. (00:42:11): I'm making this set up, right. 80% of the folks that I work with, this is their biggest problem. Even at executive levels, they'll ask their team, or teams will come back with uncertainty, and they'll say like, "Well, you told me to improve developer experience." I'm like, "Okay, great. What do you mean by that?" And then teams will have gone off for several months, and they're tackling something, and they'll come back, and they'll be like, "Oh, well, wasn't what I meant." (00:42:38): And I'm like, "Okay, what do you mean by this? Are you talking about inner and outer loop? Are you talking about friction? Are you talking about culture?" Because sometimes they're talking about culture. "And if you're talking about culture, this is an incredibly valid answer. But if you're talking about culture, this is totally different than if you're talking about friction in toolchains, right. And if you're on different pages, you're heading in completely different directions." (00:43:05): So that's one thing we cover, which seems obvious, but trust me, it's not. And then even how do you... We're going to do kind of a rough version of how do you start measuring from nothing and also the measurement journey, right. How do you think about the trade-offs between and the proportion of measurement between subjective data, right, data from people. So you have Azure interviews, and you have surveys and objective data, stuff you get from systems. Because when you first start off, you'll be relying much more on data from people. (00:43:42): You can get a relatively quickly. But as you kind of transition through this measurement journey, you'll get more and more data from your systems because it's scalable. It can be engineered. You can be doing much more with it. And also, you should be thinking about, "Don't let the perfect be the enemy of the good." So how do we think about this very, very strategically? How do we transition through this? How do we think about what each piece of data is for? (00:44:09): And also lots and lots of examples. So I have included example interview scripts. How do you select people? How do you screen people? Example survey scripts. What are some of the analyses we should do? And trying to make this incredibly accessible, so basically anyone can do this. So you do not need to be a data scientist, but if you have one on staff, you can hand them some of this and just let them run.
turns.zh: 对，绝对。就像我提到的，当某个问题被问得很频繁时，我倾向于把它写下来。所以这一本尤其如此。所以我们将会覆盖……我开始过一遍，我在覆盖其中一些，而我觉得其中一些重要的话题，特别是从"你的问题是什么、你的目标是什么"开始，并且对它超级超级清晰，对吧。我们到底想回答什么？而我会说这是一个比大多数人认识到或意识到的更大的挑战。 (00:42:11)：我在做这个铺垫，对吧。我合作的人里 80% 都把这个问题当成他们最大的问题。即使在高管层面，他们会问他们的团队，或者团队会带着不确定性回来，说类似"好吧，你让我去改善开发者体验。"我就说"好，太好了。你这话是什么意思？"然后团队会花几个月去搞某个东西，然后带着结果回来，说"哦，好吧，那不是我意思的那东西。" (00:42:38)：然后我就说"好，你这话是什么意思？你说的是内循环还是外循环？你说的是摩擦？你说的是文化？"因为有时他们说的是文化。"而如果你说的是文化，那是个极其合理的答案。但如果你说的是文化，那和你说的工具链里的摩擦完全是两回事，对吧。如果你们不在同一个频道上，你们就走向完全不同的方向。"(00:43:05)：所以那是我们覆盖的一件事，它看起来显而易见，但相信我，它不是。然后甚至是你怎么……我们会做一个粗略版——你怎么从零开始衡量，以及衡量的旅程，对吧。你怎么思考主观数据（也就是来自人的数据）之间的权衡和比例。所以你有 Azure 访谈，你有调查，还有客观数据，也就是你从系统得到的东西。因为你刚开始时，你会更依赖来自人的数据。 (00:43:42)：你可以相对快地得到它。但当你穿过这个衡量旅程时，你会从你的系统得到越来越多的数据，因为它是可扩展的。它可以被工程化。你可以用它做更多事。而且，你应该思考"别让完美成为好的敌人（Don't let the perfect be the enemy of the good）。"所以我们怎么非常非常战略性地思考这个？我们怎么穿过这个？我们怎么思考每一块数据是用来干嘛的？ (00:44:09)：还有大量大量的例子。所以我包含了示例访谈脚本。你怎么选人？你怎么筛选人？示例调查脚本。我们应该做哪些分析？并试图让这个极其容易上手，所以基本上任何人都能做这个。所以你不需要是数据科学家，但如果你员工里有一个，你可以把其中一些交给他们，让他们直接跑。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: What are the most common pitfalls that companies run into when they're trying to roll out any sort of developer experience, developer productivity, system measurements, improvements?
turns.zh: 公司在尝试推出任何形式的开发者体验、开发者生产力、系统测量、改进时，最常遇到的陷阱是什么？

turns.speaker: Nicole Forsgren
turns.en: I think one I just mentioned, right. Not being clear or not understanding what it is that they're looking for because then you can have a thousand flowers bloom, and everyone's kind of running in a different direction. I think another one is not pursuing this in both a top-down and a bottom-up structure, right. And I think that can really help drive success, and having good communication throughout is super, super important, right. (00:46:26): So getting your ICs bought in and helping them understand that this is for them. We want to understand what they're doing. Knowing what vocabulary they use, what terminology they use is super important. And then chatting with leaders and understanding what their motivations are or helping them understand what the motivations could be. This kind of hearkens back to one of our earliest chats on why I even got into this and how I see two different sides to the conversation on why is DevOps even a thing? Why should we even ship faster? (00:47:03): There are so many people that I talk to that are super passionate about DevX right now, and they're like, "How can I convince my executive team this is important?" Because their developers are just completely burning out, or they use computers and anger every day. And so it's like, "How can we have the right tools to socialize this to our leaders as well?" Because this should be a priority. This needs to be a strategic piece, and how can we help pull together the right value points to communicate this and to understand what their priorities are so that we can see how this fits in, right.
turns.zh: 我觉得一个我刚提到的，对吧。不清楚或不理解他们在找什么，因为那样你就会"百花齐放"，每个人都朝不同方向跑。我觉得另一个是没有以自上而下和自下而上双重结构来推进这个，对吧。而我觉得那能真的帮驱动成功，并且全程有良好的沟通是超级超级重要的，对吧。 (00:46:26)：所以让你的 IC（个人贡献者，individual contributors）买账，帮他们理解这是为他们做的。我们想理解他们在做什么。知道他们用什么词汇、什么术语是超级重要的。然后和领导者聊、理解他们的动机是什么、或者帮他们理解动机可能是什么。这有点呼应我们最早的一次聊天——关于我当初为什么进入这个领域，以及我怎么看到关于"DevOps 甚至是个东西吗？我们为什么甚至要更快地交付？"的对话有两面。 (00:47:03)：我和太多现在对 DevX 超级热情的人聊过，他们说"我怎么说服我的高管团队这很重要？"因为他们的开发者正在彻底 burnout，或者他们每天带着愤怒用电脑。所以就像是"我们怎么也有合适的工具把这个社会化（socialize）给我们的领导者？"因为这应该是一个优先事项。这需要是一个战略性的部分，而我们怎么帮着把正确的价值点拉到一起、去沟通这个、并理解他们的优先级是什么，这样我们就能看到这怎么契合进去，对吧。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: You've been working in this space for a long time, probably longer than anyone that has ever worked on this area of developer experience productivity. What have you seen change most from the time you started working in the space to today? What kind of progress has been made?
turns.zh: 你在这个领域工作很长时间了，大概比任何曾在这个开发者体验生产力领域工作过的人都久。从你开始在这个领域工作到今天，你看到什么变化最大？取得了什么样的进展？

turns.speaker: Nicole Forsgren
turns.en: We have these increasingly large complex systems, right. So 10 or 15 years ago, the internet was around, but things were really different. Now, almost every company has a really large complex system, right. We also have a shortage of developers, or at least a reported perceived shortage of developers. More companies are technology-driven, or at least they understand they're technology driven. It's like I understand a handful... I remember a handful of years ago when I met with a financial institution whose CTO insisted to me that he was not a tech company like that. That's not real anymore. That doesn't happen anymore, at least very, very rarely. (00:48:39): So all of these things come together, and suddenly, many more companies are like, "We have to be better at this." And that was not always the case five to 10 years ago. I used to have to really explain why this was a pressing concern and why it would continue to be a oppressing concern. And now, in the last six to nine to 12 months, we have this AI moment happening, and it just poured gas on top of everything because now what's important... We've always said that [inaudible 00:49:14] execution's important, but now this is absolutely true because it's not just about what it is that you build. (00:49:23): It's about creating absolutely novel, incredibly new experiences and doing them at a speed that no one has seen before. And the only way to do this is to have this software pipeline that is fast and is safe and is stable, and is reliable. And that's where we're seeing this really interesting convergence, and pressure isn't quite the right word, but it's really forcing the discussion and strategy and prioritization, right.
turns.zh: 我们有这些越来越大的复杂系统，对吧。所以 10 或 15 年前，互联网是存在的，但事情真的很不一样。现在，几乎每家公司都有一个真正大的复杂系统，对吧。我们也有开发者短缺，或者至少是被报道的、感知到的开发者短缺。更多公司是技术驱动的，或者至少他们理解他们是技术驱动的。就像我记得几年前，当我遇到一家金融机构，它的 CTO 坚持对我说他不是那种科技公司。那不再是真的了。那不会再发生了，至少非常非常罕见了。 (00:48:39)：所以所有这些东西凑到一起，突然间，更多公司像"我们必须在这方面做得更好。"而这在五到十年前并不总是这样。我以前必须真的解释为什么这是个紧迫的关切、以及为什么它会继续是个压迫性的（oppressing）关切。而现在，在过去六到九到十二个月里，我们有了这个 AI 时刻在发生，它只是把汽油浇到了一切之上，因为现在重要的……我们一直说 [inaudible 00:49:14] 执行很重要，但现在这绝对是真的，因为这不只是关于你构建的是什么。 (00:49:23)：它是关于创造绝对新颖、极其全新的体验，并且以没人见过的速度去做。而做到这一点的唯一方式，是拥有这个既快又安全、又稳定的软件流水线，并且可靠。而那就是我们看到这种真正有趣的汇聚（convergence）的地方，pressure（压力）不是完全正确的词，但它真的在迫使关于讨论、战略和优先级的思考，对吧。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: I'm glad you touched on AI. That was actually exactly where I was going to go next.
turns.zh: 我很高兴你提到了 AI。那其实正是我接下来要去的。

turns.speaker: Nicole Forsgren
turns.en: Perfect.
turns.zh: 完美。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Yeah, obviously productivity, AI, engineering, something that's top of mind for a lot of people. There's a lot of layoffs that have been happening. There's a lot of talk of we don't need as many engineers. I actually had dinner not too long ago with few, I'd say 10 X engineers, and those are folks that people sometimes say they don't need Copilot. They're not going to use any of these tools. They're already amazing. And they were the opposite. (00:50:34): They're like, "This is making me 100% more effective and efficient and I love it." So clearly good things are happening there. I don't know what the question is specifically, but I guess have you seen the impact of AI on engineering productivity? And has that shifted how you think about developer experience and productivity beyond what you already just shared?
turns.zh: 对，显然生产力、AI、工程，是很多人心里最关心的事。现在有大量裁员在发生。有很多关于"我们不需要那么多工程师"的讨论。其实不久之前我和几个——我会说是 10 倍（10X）工程师——吃了顿饭，那些人有时人们说他们不需要 Copilot。他们不会用任何这些工具。他们已经很厉害了。而他们恰恰相反。 (00:50:34)：他们像"这让我有效率和效果提升了 100%，我爱死它了。"所以显然那里有好事在发生。我不知道具体的问题是什么，但我想，你有没有看到 AI 对工程生产力的影响？而且它是否改变了你怎么思考开发者体验和生产力——超出你刚才已经分享的？

turns.speaker: Nicole Forsgren
turns.en: Absolutely. So yes and, right.
turns.zh: 绝对。所以是的，但也不完全是，对吧。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Mm-hmm.
turns.zh: 嗯。

turns.speaker: Nicole Forsgren
turns.en: I think this is a super interesting open question. So can I answer it just with a whole bunch of questions?
turns.zh: 我觉得这是个超级有趣的开放问题。所以我能不能用一大堆问题来回答它？

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Absolutely.
turns.zh: 绝对。

turns.speaker: Nicole Forsgren
turns.en: We're absolutely seeing an impact, and we continue to explore this. So I have an interesting question to see how it'll change the SPACE framework. What's open here? I think a few things will remain, right? Satisfaction's still going to be there, performance is still going to be there, activity's still going to be there. How you communicate with people and with the tool efficiency and flow is still going to be there. I believe it will change and add a dimension like trust or reliability. How do I rely? Can I rely on it? (00:51:35): Will I have an over-reliance on it? And what we're seeing is that, probably unsurprisingly, people really fundamentally shift the way they work when they work with an AI-enabled tool like GitHub, Copilot, or Tabnine or others because now, instead of just writing code or having a short auto-complete, you spend more time reviewing code than writing code, right. There's this wonderful paper out that uses the Cups model. I'll share it with you. A team at MSR did it. Defines it, "About 50% of your time now is spent reviewing versus writing." But it'll be interesting to see how that changes things longitudinally, right. (00:52:20): Because other... Some of my colleagues also did a paper that showed that you can do certain tasks, like build an HTTP server 50% faster, but I don't think that's what productivity's about when you're using an AI tool, frankly. Anyone who's looking at that and dear CEOs or whoever who are like, "Now I can lay off half my workforce." That's not what this is about, right. It's not about taking a task and cutting your time in half because now what we've enabled is your ability to do certain things faster and then free up some of your cognitive space so that you can do harder things with this new co-pilot sidecar or something, right. (00:53:03): But also, because now you're accepting text and then reviewing it, we've changed what your mental model is. So we've changed the friction model that you expect. We've changed the cognitive load of what you expect. We're changing reliance on code. So what does this mean for reliance or overreliance? What does this mean for learning? What does this mean for novices versus experts? How do we measure productivity, right? There are a handful of us that are having these discussions on what does this mean and how do we communicate it thoughtfully? (00:53:35): Again, we really need to have these kind of holistic, balanced metrics because if it's an oversimplification, we really risk losing the forest for the trees, right. But it's also super interesting and super compelling, I think. How can we think about learning or onboarding to new code bases or new languages for folks who already know computational learning? I think it's also very different for folks who are just learning programming languages and don't already know things like computational thinking.
turns.zh: 我们绝对看到了影响，而且我们持续在探索这个。所以我有一个有趣的问题，看它会怎么改变 SPACE 框架。什么是开放的？我觉得有几样东西会保留，对吧？满意度还会在，绩效还会在，活动还会在。你怎么和人沟通、以及和工具的效率与流畅度也都还会在。我相信它会改变、并增加一个像信任或可靠性这样的维度。我怎么依赖？我能依赖它吗？ (00:51:35)：我会有过度依赖吗？而我们看到的是，大概不出所料，当人们和像 GitHub、Copilot、或 Tabnine 这样的 AI 驱动工具一起工作时，他们真的从根本上改变了工作方式，因为现在，不再只是写代码或有个简短的自动补全，你花在审查代码上的时间比写代码多，对吧。有一篇很棒的论文用了 Cups 模型。我会分享给你。MSR 的一个团队做的。它定义说"现在大约 50% 的时间花在审查而不是写。"但纵向地看那会怎么改变事情会很有趣，对吧。 (00:52:20)：因为其他……我的一些同事也写了一篇论文，显示你能做某些任务，比如快 50% 地搭一个 HTTP 服务器，但我坦白说，我不认为那是用 AI 工具时生产力是关于什么的。任何看那个的人、以及亲爱的 CEO 们或谁，像"现在我能裁掉我一半的劳动力。"那不是这关于什么的，对吧。它不是关于拿一个任务、把你的时间砍半，因为现在我们启用的是你更快做某些事的能力，然后腾出你的一些认知空间，这样你能用这个新的 co-pilot 副驾（sidecar）或类似的东西去做更难的事，对吧。 (00:53:03)：但还有，因为现在你接受文本然后审查它，我们改变了你的心智模型是什么。所以我们改变了你预期的摩擦模型。我们改变了你预期的认知负荷。我们在改变对代码的依赖。所以这对依赖或过度依赖意味着什么？这对学习意味着什么？这对新手 vs 专家意味着什么？我们怎么衡量生产力，对吧？我们中有少数人在进行这些讨论——这意味着什么、我们怎么有思想地沟通它？ (00:53:35)：再次，我们真的需要有这种整体的、平衡的指标，因为如果它是过度简化，我们真的有失去森林只见树木的风险，对吧。但我也觉得它超级有趣、超级引人入胜。我们怎么思考学习、或者对新代码库或新语言的上手（onboarding）——对已经懂计算学习（computational learning）的人？我觉得对那些刚开始学编程语言、还不懂像计算思维（computational thinking）这种东西的人，也非常不同。

turns.en: Sounds like something you could do in a day.

turns.speaker: Nicole Forsgren

turns.zh: 有没有哪些公司是你看作好榜样的——"他们这个做得真的很好"？

turns.speaker: Nicole Forsgren
turns.en: I think Google does this incredibly well, and sometimes I hesitate to mention Google because they're like... some people are like, "Well, we can't be Google, and we aren't really advanced." But the thing I love about Google's approach is that they've really taken kind of this measurement phase approach to things, even when they roll it out in new places. They're very systematic in how they measure things. (00:55:41): They have incredible telemetry and tooling and instrumentation, and they continue to invest time in developer experience surveys and they triangulate them. And one thing that I also love being able to point out here is if there is ever a disagreement between the surveys and the instrumentation, which is incredibly advanced, almost every time, every that I've ever heard of the surveys are correct and not the instrumentation.
turns.zh: 我觉得 Google 做得不可思议地好，而有时我犹豫提 Google，因为他们像……有些人像"好吧，我们成不了 Google，我们也没那么先进。"但我爱的 Google 做法的一点是，他们真的把这种"测量先行"的方式用在了事情上，即使是在新地方推出时。他们在怎么衡量事情上非常系统化。 (00:55:41)：他们有不可思议的遥测（telemetry）、工具和埋点，并且他们持续投入时间在开发者体验调查上，并且对它们做三角印证（triangulate）。而我也爱能在这里指出的一点是，如果调查和埋点之间出现分歧——而埋点是极其先进的——几乎每一次、我听说过的每一次，都是调查是对的、而不是埋点。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Amazing. I have just a couple more questions unrelated to this topic. Is there anything else that you thought you think would be useful to share or leave people with around this general space?
turns.zh: 太棒了。我还有几个和这个话题无关的问题。在这个通用领域里，还有什么你觉得有用的、想分享或留给人们的东西吗？

turns.en: I would say that thinking about what it is you want to do is always important, right. Like getting crisp, the ability to communicate clearly is always one of the best things. I think one of my superpowers and one of the things that I've been working with my teams on doing and kind of teaching them is, and one of the things that's really leveled up our work in general, is making your work incredibly accessible. (00:56:49): And accessible, not necessarily in the accessibility definition of the word, but making it very easy to understand what you're doing for your key audiences. And so thinking about doing that for anything that... anyone who's listening for all of your work is super important, right. So who is it that your audience is? What's their role? What words resonate with them? And then always being able to translate your work into a few sentences or a paragraph or left... or less.
turns.zh: 我会说，想清楚你想做什么，总是重要的，对吧。比如变得清晰，清晰沟通的能力总是最好的事情之一。我觉得我的超能力之一、也是我一直在和我的团队做、并教他们的一件事——而这也是真正让我们整体工作升级的一件事——是让你的工作极其容易理解（accessible）。 (00:56:49)：而 accessible 不一定是那个词在"无障碍"意义上的定义，而是让你的关键受众非常容易理解你在做什么。所以为任何事情思考这个……任何在听的、为你们所有的工作思考这个，都超级重要，对吧。所以你的受众是谁？他们的角色是什么？什么词能和他们产生共鸣？然后总是能把你的工作翻译成几句话、或一段、或更少。

turns.en: I love it. A lot of the listeners of this podcast are product managers, and this is so core to the work of a PM, so I think this is [inaudible 00:57:28]-

turns.speaker: Nicole Forsgren
turns.en: Perfect.
turns.zh: 完美。

I'm curious what that is and what it's all about.
turns.zh: ……直接说到很多听众心坎里。好。所以就再问几个问题。在这期播客之前，我问了你几个问题，包括人们经常向你寻求哪方面的建议，以及还有没有你觉得真的有用的其他框架？所以有几件事我想聊一下，看看那里有没有有趣的东西。第一个是你有一个你叫"四框框架"（four-box framework）的框架。我好奇那是什么、关于什么的。

turns.speaker: Nicole Forsgren
turns.en: Yes. I love this four-box framework. I've used it for years. I actually pulled it out first when I was a professor, and I still to this day get LinkedIn messages from my students saying that it's like the most useful thing they've ever used. So here's what it is. I literally pull this out on napkins, at bars, at conferences to this day. (00:58:12): So here we go. Draw four boxes on a piece of paper, two on the top, two on the bottom. So they'll be kind of aligned. The first two to the left of them write the word words. And below them, write the word data and then between the two on the top, draw an arrow between them. So it'll say words, box, arrow, box, right. Is that making sense?
turns.zh: 对。我爱这个四框框架。我用了很多年。我其实第一次掏出它是在我当教授的时候，而直到今天我还收到我学生的 LinkedIn 消息，说它就像他们用过最有用的东西。所以这是它是什么。我 literally 到现在还在餐巾纸、酒吧、会议上掏出它。 (00:58:12)：所以来吧。在一张纸上画四个框，上面两个，下面两个。所以它们会大致对齐。前两个左边写"words（文字）"这个词。在它们下面，写"data（数据）"这个词，然后在上面两个之间，画一个箭头。所以它会是 words、框、箭头、框，对吧。这说得通吗？

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Mm-hmm.
turns.zh: 嗯。

turns.speaker: Nicole Forsgren
turns.en: And then on the bottom it'll say data, box, arrow, box.
turns.zh: 然后下面会是 data、框、箭头、框。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Mm-hmm.
turns.zh: 嗯。

turns.speaker: Nicole Forsgren
turns.en: Okay. So on the top half, this is where, if you want to think about measuring something or testing something, you have to start with words. So as an example, let's just say, I think that customer satisfaction gets us more money or customer satisfaction gets us return customers. Let's do customer satisfaction. So the first box, you'll put customer satisfaction inside the box, and you'll put return customers in the second box. Now always start with words. You do not start with data. You always start with words. (00:59:22): And then you'll go around to a couple of people, stakeholders, managers, others, and you'll say, "Do you agree with this? Is this actually what we're doing?" And it can turn into a sentence. And then, in the boxes below it, this is your data. How are we going to measure customer satisfaction? It could be a survey. (00:59:44): And so this is where you'll go, and you'll say, "What data points do we have that could proxy for? What could be our data points for customer satisfaction?" And this is where it gets tricky. You could say, "Well, customer satisfaction could be return customers. But we think it leads to return customers, so we can't use that here." But return customers could be... So that's where you kind of roll this out. So how else would we measure customer satisfaction? I made this hard on myself.
turns.zh: 好。所以在上半部分，这是——如果你想衡量或测试某个东西，你必须从文字开始。所以举个例子，我们就说，我认为客户满意度（customer satisfaction）给我们带来更多钱、或者客户满意度给我们带来回头客（return customers）。我们做客户满意度。所以第一个框，你把客户满意度放进框里，你把回头客放进第二个框。现在总是从文字开始。你不从数据开始。你总是从文字开始。 (00:59:22)：然后你会去找几个人、干系人、经理、其他人，你会说"你同意这个吗？这真的是我们在做的吗？"它能变成一句话。然后，在它下面的框里，这是你的数据。我们要怎么衡量客户满意度？可以是调查。 (00:59:44)：所以这是你会去的地方，你会说"我们有哪些数据点可以作为代理（proxy）？我们的客户满意度的数据点可能是什么？"而这就是它变 tricky 的地方。你可能会说"嗯，客户满意度可以是回头客。但我们认为它导致回头客，所以我们不能在这里用它。"但回头客可以是……所以那就是你大概铺开它的地方。那我们还能怎么衡量客户满意度？我给自己出了个难题。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Like a CSAT score or NPS score.
turns.zh: 像 CSAT 分数或 NPS 分数。

turns.speaker: Nicole Forsgren
turns.en: CSAT. Yeah.
turns.zh: CSAT。对。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Yeah.
turns.zh: 对。

turns.speaker: Nicole Forsgren
turns.en: CSAT, NPS.
turns.zh: CSAT、NPS。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Mm-hmm.
turns.zh: 嗯。

turns.speaker: Nicole Forsgren
turns.en: We could say the amount of money that they spent. It's a stretch.
turns.zh: 我们可以说他们花的钱的数量。那有点牵强。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Mm-hmm.
turns.zh: 嗯。

turns.speaker: Nicole Forsgren
turns.en: Okay. Now, return customers. Let's go to the next box. How are we going to measure return customers? Depending on our context, let's say that this is an online business. We could say that it's return customers as measured through the website. We could say that it's returned customers. We could just ask them, right. Maybe we have a follow-up survey. Return customers. Maybe we're going to do a stretch here. Maybe we say it's a referral link. This helps us get super clear on what it is we're going to measure. Now, the reason I like this is because if some of our... Now this data analysis. We'll just do correlations here, right. (01:01:00): If we have longitudinal overtime, that's fine. You can hand this to a data scientist. You can hand this to someone and you can say, "What data do we have? Let's go run this." If something here falls apart, now you can point to the data boxes, and we can get mad about the things in the data boxes, and we can say, "What's wrong? Is the data poor quality? Are we missing data? Was this a bad proxy?" Proxy stands in for something else. "Was this ridiculous?" One of the things I made up. It was just a bad idea. (01:01:32): Instead of getting mad at Lenny for his really stupid idea or getting mad at Nicole because this was a really bad idea, we can say, "This was problematic. What's wrong here?" Or we can go back up to the words at the top, and we can say, "This is not actually something that is probably going to hold, or this is not something we want to test right now, or this is something instead..." turns.zh: 好。现在，回头客。我们去下一个框。我们要怎么衡量回头客？取决于我们的情境，假设这是个线上业务。我们可以说它是通过网站衡量的回头客。我们可以说它是 returned customers。我们可以直接问他们，对吧。也许我们有个后续调查。回头客。也许我们要在这里牵强一下。也许我们说它是个推荐链接（referral link）。这帮我们超级清楚我们要衡量的是什么。现在，我喜欢这个的原因是，因为如果我们的某些……现在这个数据分析。我们就在这里做相关性（correlations），对吧。 (01:01:00)：如果我们有纵向的随时间数据，那没问题。你可以把这个交给数据科学家。你可以交给某人，说"我们有什么数据？我们去跑这个。"如果这里有什么崩了，现在你可以指向数据框，我们可以对数据框里的东西发火，我们可以说"什么错了？数据质量差吗？我们缺数据吗？这是个坏的代理（proxy）吗？"Proxy 是代替别的东西。"这很荒谬吗？"我编的其中之一。那只是个坏主意。 (01:01:32)：而不是对 Lenny 因为他真的很蠢的主意发火、或者因为 Nicole 这是个坏主意而对 Nicole 发火，我们可以说"这有问题。这里什么错了？"或者我们可以回到顶上的文字，我们可以说"这实际上不是个大概能站得住的东西，或者这不是我们现在想测试的，或者这是别的东西……"而这让事情极其清晰。它帮你相当快地沟通你想做什么。
